note: Rav and Rabba bar bar Hana were sitting together when a man passed by wearing a cloak made entirely of sky-blue wool, with white and sky-blue ritual fringes that were wound all the way down, with no loose strands hanging. Rav said the cloak was beautiful but the fringes were not. Rabba bar bar Hana said both the cloak and the fringes were beautiful.
why: The Gemara has just set rules for how the fringe strings are wound; their two remarks become a disagreement over whether fringes must also have loose strings hanging below the windings, which the Gemara then traces to two verses.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who said the cloak was beautiful but the fringes were not.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: A Sage sitting with Rav who said both the cloak and the fringes were beautiful.

terms.meaning: Strings the Torah requires on the corners of a four-cornered garment (tzitzit), including a sky-blue thread.
A blue dye (tekhelet) the Torah requires for one thread of the fringes.
Sets of coils wrapped around the fringe strings near the garment.

note: The Sages told Rabbi Perida that Rabbi Ezra, a descendant of Ezra the Scribe through a long line of famous Sages, was waiting at his gate. Rabbi Perida asked why they were listing his ancestors: a man of Torah is worthy on his own, but a man of lineage without Torah, "better for fire to devour him" than enter. Told that Ezra was a man of Torah, he let him in. Seeing Ezra was troubled, Rabbi Perida taught a homily praising the Patriarchs as those whom God credits. Hearing the word "excellent" (addir), Rabbi Ezra replied with a series of wordplay homilies on addir, yadid (beloved), "good" and "this," each tying Moses, Solomon, Abraham, the Torah, the Temple, God and Israel together.
why: Rabbi Perida has just appeared in the discussion asking where meal offerings get their rule against leavening, so the Gemara attaches this incident about him.

people.name: Rabbi Perida
people.about: A Sage at whose house Rabbi Ezra waited; he insisted that Torah learning, not lineage, makes a man worthy.

people.name: Rabbi Ezra
people.about: A Sage descended from Ezra the Scribe, who answered Rabbi Perida with homilies of his own.

people.name: Ezra
people.about: Ezra the Scribe, Rabbi Ezra's ancestor.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: A Sage in Rabbi Ezra's family line, descended from Ezra the Scribe.

people.name: Rabbi Avtolus
people.about: Rabbi Ezra's grandfather, a descendant of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.

terms.meaning: A sermon-like reading of Bible verses that draws a lesson from wording, often through wordplay.
Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the founding fathers of the Jewish people.

note: Three women brought three pairs of birds as offerings. One said hers was "for my ziva," one "for my yamma," and one "for my ona." The Sages took all three to mean bleeding and purification, so each would bring a sin offering and a burnt offering. Mordekhai suggested instead that one had been in danger from a flow, one at sea (yam), and one through her eye (ayin), so all three were thanksgiving burnt offerings. It was checked, and Mordekhai was found to be right.
why: The Gemara has just told how Mordekhai decoded a deaf-mute's gestures to find grain for the Temple; this is a further example of his skill with words, and leads to identifying him with Petahya, who was in charge of bird offerings.

people.name: Mordekhai
people.about: A Sage who read the women's words differently from the other Sages and was found to be right.

terms.meaning: Pairs of pigeons or doves brought as offerings, for example by a woman after certain kinds of bleeding.
A woman with a discharge of blood outside her normal period, who must bring an offering when she is purified.
A sin offering atones for a specific state or wrong; a burnt offering is burned whole on the altar and can also be a voluntary gift.

note: Rabbi Tarfon sat puzzling over why meal offerings from new grain brought before the omer are unfit, while those brought before the two loaves are fit. Yehuda ben Nehemya answered him with a distinction, Rabbi Tarfon fell silent, and the young man's face lit up. Rabbi Akiva said to him: "Yehuda, has your face brightened because you answered the elder? I will be astonished if your life is long." Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Ilai reported that this happened two weeks before Passover; when he came back for Shavuot and asked about Yehuda ben Nehemya, he was told he had died.
why: The mishna rules that offerings from new grain brought before the omer are unfit but those brought between the omer and the two loaves are fit; the incident gives the reasoning for that difference, which Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak then extends to fruit.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: An elder Sage who raised the question and fell silent at the answer.

people.name: Yehuda ben Nehemya
people.about: A Sage who answered Rabbi Tarfon and looked pleased; he died soon afterward.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who rebuked Yehuda ben Nehemya for gloating over answering the elder.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda, son of Rabbi Ilai
people.about: A Sage who tells when the incident happened and that Yehuda ben Nehemya died.

terms.meaning: A measure of new barley offered in the Temple on the second day of Passover; only after it may the new crop be eaten.
Two wheat loaves offered on Shavuot, after which the new crop may be used for Temple offerings.
An offering of flour, usually mixed with oil, brought in the Temple.

note: Shimon HaTzaddik, the High Priest, foresaw his death: each Yom Kippur an old man in white had entered the Holy of Holies with him and left with him, but this year he was in black and did not leave. He died after Sukkot, naming his son Onias as successor. In Rabbi Meir's telling, Onias's older brother Shimi, jealous, tricked Onias into a tunic and ribbon and told the priests it was a vow to his lover; the priests wanted to kill Onias, who fled to Alexandria and built an altar for idol worship. Rabbi Yehuda says it was the reverse: Onias declined the post, then grew jealous and played the trick on Shimi; when exposed he fled to Alexandria and built an altar to God. The Sages drew a lesson about jealousy over high office.
why: The mishna implies the temple of Onias in Egypt was not for idol worship; this baraita is cited because Rabbi Yehuda's version supports that view, while Rabbi Meir's says it was.

people.name: Shimon HaTzaddik
people.about: A High Priest who foresaw his own death and named his son Onias to succeed him.

people.name: Onias
people.about: Son of Shimon HaTzaddik, who built an altar in Alexandria in Egypt.

people.name: Shimi
people.about: Onias's brother, two and a half years older than him.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage whose version says Onias's altar was for idol worship.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who says the incident went otherwise and Onias's altar was for God.

terms.meaning: The innermost room of the Temple, which only the High Priest entered, on Yom Kippur.
The blessing the priests recite over the people; in the Temple it was said with God's own name.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the mishna.
